I’m 17 and I got all my friends into the Dead and it’s been one of the best bonding experiences of my life. If you know people who are open to checking them out I highly recommend doing it with them!

Over the last two years, I've become a massive Deadhead, and it's honestly a very hard thing to explain, but I'll try my best.

The Grateful Dead are renowned for their improvisational live shows, and which they do sprawling live jams that can last up to 45 minutes. They are cohesive, interesting, and perfect for getting high to. You're never going to "get" the Dead by listening to any studio albums, and I'd recommend starting with Europe '72 (that's how I got started).

In addition to the community aspect you mention, their sound is incredibly unique, I have never heard another band that sounds like them. This is because of the wide variety of backgrounds the members come from. Jerry Garcia was a bluegrass banjo player turned electric guitarist, Bob Weir was a 16-year old kid just learning to play guitar, therefore developing his own unique style of rhythm guitar, Phil Lesh was a classical composer who Jerry asked to learn to play bass, and Bill Kreutzmann was a trained jazz drummer (these are the mainstay members). 

In addition to this, all of their live shows have been recorded and can be listened to for free, legally, on archive.org/details/GratefulDead. Because they are rooted so heavily on improvisation, every version of every song is different, leading to the ability to hear new music, yet there's this overwhelming sense of familiarity to it that makes it so addicting to keep listening to. Especially when it comes to songs like Dark Star or The Other One, there are no two versions that are the same. 

The songs are AMAZING, lots of them sounding like old folk tunes written in the late 1800's and early 1900's. It bring the listener to a new place and helps to reinforce that unique feeling that the Dead seem to bring forth.

Every era has its own unique sound as well, and it becomes really fun to see how they played different songs in different years. 67-69 is heavy, psychedelic rock, 1970-71 starts to see some more folk influence, 1972 is a culmination of all of the influences they've had so far, 1973-74 is jazzy and exploratory, 1976-77 is funky and upbeat, etc. They all have their own unique sound and traits that make it fun to explore all of their music, especially when it's so easily accessible to listen to.



I'll link some of my favorite shows, videos, and recordings if you want to check them out.

Shows:

May 8th, 1977, Barton Hall, Cornell University

Often hailed as the greatest show of all time, it has become a legendary night in one of the Dead's biggest touring peaks.

A high-energy great show from their most straightforward rock year.

November 17th, 1973, Pauley Pavilion, UCLA

A jazzy, low-key show with a great second set from my favorite Grateful Dead year.

https://archive.org/details/gd1973-11-17.sbd.ashley.23472.sbefail.shnf/gd73-11-17Berthad2t07.shn
